you were working on this: Also, lets address those issues you highlighted please? ```**Root cause:** the discriminator should be *discovered*, not hard-coded — look for a property common to all members whose value is a distinct `const`. `method` works for the request unions. Where no member pins a const (2026-07-28's `resultType` is free-form), the untagged fallback is unsafe as-is: the generic `Result` member must sort most-specific-first, or the generator should fail the build rather than emit a union that silently mis-assigns.

This is the same bug class `content_member_order.rs` documents — but the fix that landed (tag dispatch) only covers unions discriminated by `type`, and the arm-level test only covers the 5 content unions out of 65.

## Two smaller gaps

**Feature-matrix citations.** 39 variants: 32 cite a revision, 12 an SEP number, **1 a URL**. AGENTS.md requires "a doc comment with the URL". `every_row_is_cited_and_ordered` (`feature.rs:1184`) only checks that the revision is known and ordered — the name over-promises.

**Verification coverage is 9%.** The property suite covers 62 of 708 (revision, definition) pairs. `generation.rs` checks the structural contract across the whole surface; value-level round-trip is checked on 9%. The arm-level test covers 5 of 65 tagged unions.```

commit c22bfd84844ec675fc43550796f0eddb7c28bb3a
Author: Nick Campbell <s0ma@protonmail.com>
Date:   Tue Nov 3 12:37:27 2026 -0500

    fix(schema): dispatch union arms on the member that tells them apart
    
    Every generated wire union picked its arm by member order, which meant a
    `tools/call` request decoded as an `InitializeRequest` and a 2026-07-28
    server result landed in the generic `Result` arm. The misplacement was
    silent: every generated type carries a `#[serde(flatten)]` catch-all, so
    a value decoded into the wrong arm re-serialises to byte-identical JSON.
    
    A union now dispatches two ways. Where the specification requires a
    member of every alternative — `type` for content blocks, `method` for
    requests and notifications — that member is read and an absent or unknown
    value is a decode error rather than a guess. Where no such member
    exists, the arm is chosen by the shape of the value: the arm's JSON kind,
    the members it requires, and the properties two or more arms pin to
    different values. The arm accounting for more of the value wins, and the
    specification's own order breaks a tie.
    
    A discriminator has to be *required* by every alternative, not merely
    pinned by it. `ElicitRequestParams` pins `mode` to `form` and to `url`
    but only the URL alternative requires it, so a form elicitation sent
    without the tag is a value the specification accepts and a dispatcher
    that insists on reading the tag would reject it.
    
    The new `union_arm_selection` test covers all 112 unions across all six
    revisions, building each alternative's value from the schema rather than
    from a hand-written fixture, and asserts which arm was selected. Where
    two alternatives produce byte-identical values, it asserts the weaker
    invariant that still holds: the selected arm must be one that accepts
    the value.

  an error.** The crate-root expectation was fulfilled under
  `--all-features` and unfulfilled under the default set, and
  `unfulfilled_lint_expectations` is deny-by-default. So the fix could not
  be "make the expectation conditional on the feature set" — it had to be
  "stop needing the expectation". Conditional expectations are a trap: they
  encode a fact about the build matrix that the compiler only checks in one
  of its cells.
- **The fix was the tests, not a narrower suppression.** `utcp` now has a
  test module that serves a real provider over loopback HTTP and drives
  the whole path: read the manual, refuse what the registration does not
  permit, call a tool and see the argument arrive. Twelve tests, and the
  lint has nothing left to report in any of the eight feature
  combinations the crate builds under.
- **`cargo fmt` is not in the documented preflight, and the UTCP commit was
  never formatted.** `cargo build && cargo test && cargo l && cargo deny`
  all passed on unformatted code; the `pre-push` hook's `cargo fmt --check`
  is what caught it. A preflight that omits a check is a preflight that
  does not know about a whole class of failure.
- **A test that asserts on `error.to_string()` asserts on the wrong
  string.** `anyhow`'s `Display` is the top context alone; the chain — the
  part that says *why* — is in `Debug` and in `{:#}`. The first version of
  the plain-HTTP refusal test failed because it read the top context and
  found "the provider's URL could not be used" instead of "is plain HTTP
  to `api.example.com`". A user sees the chain, so the test has to read
  the chain.


## Learnings: a union that cannot tell its arms apart (schema codegen)

The generated wire types dispatched their union arms on a hard-coded `type`
member. Where the specification pins `type` to distinct constants that works,
but most MCP unions pin something else, and the ones that pin nothing fell
back to `#[serde(untagged)]` — serde tries each member in declaration order
and keeps the first that round-trips. Every MCP request decoded into the
wrong arm (`tools/call` into `InitializeRequest`), and nothing reported it.

- **A catch-all member makes a wrong arm invisible.** Every generated type
  carries a `#[serde(flatten)]` for the members the schema does not name, so
  a value decoded into the wrong arm re-serialises to byte-identical JSON. A
  round-trip test passes for precisely the case it exists to catch. The
  assertion has to look at *which arm* was selected, not at the bytes.
- **A discriminator is only safe if the specification *requires* it.**
  `ElicitRequestParams` pins `mode` to `form` and to `url`, and both pin it
  in their own definition — but only the URL alternative *requires* it. A
  client that sends a form elicitation without the tag sends a value the
  specification accepts, and a dispatcher that insists on reading the tag
  rejects it. The rule that holds is "required by every alternative", not
  "pinned by every alternative".
- **The schema's own discriminator is not always the member that
  discriminates.** The order is `type`, `method`, `mode`, `resultType`, then
  anything else the members pin — and every alternative must pin it to a
  *distinct* value. A union whose members nest their own unions can have
  three members all tagged `string`, and no `match` on that can tell them
  apart however it is written.
- **Where no member discriminates, the shape does.** An arm is described by
  its JSON kind, the members it requires, the members it names, the shapes
  of those members, and the properties two or more arms pin to different
  values. The arm that accounts for more of the value wins; the
  specification's order breaks a tie. A constraint only one arm carries is
  that arm's own business and is not enforced by the dispatcher, because the
  generated type does not enforce it either.
- **Two alternatives can produce the same value, and then no dispatcher can
  separate them.** Four result alternatives differ only in members the schema
  does not require, so their canonical values are byte-identical. The test
  asserts the exact arm where the value is unambiguous and, where it is not,
  asserts the weaker invariant that still holds: the selected arm must be one
  that accepts the value. Asserting the exact arm there would be asserting
  something no implementation could provide.
- **The value has to be built from the schema.** Required members plus the
  members pinned to a constant, and nothing else. Adding an optional member
  makes the value look like a *different* alternative's value — `Result` and
  `SubscriptionsListenResult` both name `_meta`, and only the members one of
  them requires tell them apart. Building the value from the schema also
  means a revision that gains an alternative is covered without anyone
  remembering to add a case.
- **A schema-driven test needs the generator's own union list.** The Rust
  type name cannot be walked back to the schema, so the test carries the
  schema pointer for each union and the pointer has to resolve to an array.
  Two of the pointers did not resolve at first because a JSON pointer segment
  that names an index walks into an *array*, not an object.

## External findings (post-T29 queue)

> Issues filed by an external agent (or a human) on the `greysquirr3l/protocol-droid`
> repository while the T29 work was in flight. Tracked here so they survive a
> session roll-over, and shipped after T29 closes. Each entry is a real consumer-
> side gap with a suggested fix in the issue body; the fix is not started until
> T29 ships.

- **#10 — `HttpBuilder` cannot require authentication — only `McpRouter` can.**
  Filed by the consumer building `parlance` (an MCP server over a read-only
  QuoteWerks database, `protocol-droid` as a path dependency). The private
  `routes()` in `adapters/primary/transport/http/serve.rs` calls
  `McpRouter::new(config, sessions, handler).into_router()?` and never calls
  `with_authenticator`, so the builder path always ships an endpoint that serves
  every request under an anonymous context. `McpRouter`'s setters are wired but
  unreachable through `HttpBuilder`. Suggested fix: add
  `with_authenticator` / `with_policy` / `with_origin_policy` /
  `with_rate_limiter` pass-throughs on `HttpBuilder`, plumbed through `routes()`,
  so there is one assembly path rather than two. Optionally revisit the
  `AuthPolicy::Public` default now that T16 has shipped, or make it a required
  constructor argument on `HttpBuilder` so nobody inherits it by omission
  (breaking on a `0.1.0` crate — which makes now the cheap moment).

- **#11 — `with_authenticator` without `with_policy` fails open silently.**
  The two setters are independent: `with_authenticator` only sets the
  authenticator, `with_policy` only sets the policy, and `AuthPolicy::Public`
  is still the default in `McpRouter::new`. `refuse` short-circuits on
  `required().is_empty()`, so an unauthenticated request is served with an
  anonymous context even though the operator wired a token authenticator and
  saw no error. The unsafe combination is the easy one to reach, silent, and
  fails open. Suggested fixes (any one closes it; the last is the least
  disruptive): (1) combined `with_authenticator_and_policy(a, p)` constructor;
  (2) `with_authenticator` implies `Require`; (3) fail closed in `into_router`
  with a typed error when an authenticator has been set but the policy is still
  the default `Public` — `into_router` already returns `Result`, and
  `SecurityHeaders` already validates there for the same "starts and then
  answers with something wrong" reason. Pairs with #10: shipping #10's
  pass-throughs without addressing #11 is shipping the same trap, one level up.

- **#12 — No state injection for `#[tool]` handlers: a connection pool cannot
  reach a tool.** The `#[tool]` macro rejects a receiver outright (the error
  message points at "*an `Arc` the server holds*" as the intended solution),
  but no such channel exists. `RequestContext` carries
  `peer` / `id` / `cancel` / `progress` — no application state. `#[server]`
  generates `fn into_server(self)` and never hands the server value back to a
  tool. The available options for a consumer are all unattractive: a
  process-global (`LazyLock<Arc<T>>`), a global plus free functions, or
  bypassing `#[server]` / `#[tool]` entirely. `parlance`'s motivating case is
  a live `tiberius` connection pool that a tool handler must reach. Suggested
  fixes (roughly in increasing order of effort): (1) let `#[server]` capture
  the server value so tool handlers can close over it (matches what the macro's
  own error text already promises); (2) context-supplied `Arc<dyn Any + Send +
  Sync>` set on the `Server` at construction, with a per-call downcast; (3) a
  typed `ServerBuilder::with_state::<T>()` extension point retrievable from
  `RequestContext` as `ctx.state::<T>()`. Also worth a doc note either way: if
  the process-global is the intended answer for now, the `#[tool]` receiver
  error message should say so and the crate docs should carry a worked example
  of the pattern.

### Sequencing

T29 first. The two ACP client-side gaps (file/*, terminal/* method handling
and the notification `Stream` wrapper) are the next T29 increments; neither
touches the auth path or the `#[tool]` macro. The three external findings are
independent of T29's seam — they live in `adapters/primary/transport/http`
(#10, #11) and the macro crate (#12) — but they are real consumer-side gaps
that a single increment each is the right shape for. Once T29 is `[x]`, the
queue becomes: `#12` (smallest blast radius, isolates a single macro), then
`#10` + `#11` as one increment (they are the same pass-through, with `#11`'s
fail-closed check riding on `#10`'s setters).

# Workspace-wide cargo configuration.
#
# AGENTS.md: any warning fails the build. `build.warnings = "deny"` is the
# load-bearing Rust 1.97+ stable knob that escalates every lint warning on
# local crates to a hard build error. Two important caveats from cargo's
# docs that we accept:
#   * Only lint-class warnings are escalated — non-lint warnings (e.g. an
#     "unused config key" line) still print without failing the build. CI
#     also runs `cargo clippy -- -D warnings` to catch those.
#   * `build.warnings` is MSRV-gated; bumping rust-toolchain.toml below
#     1.97 silently turns off this gate.
[build]
# Applies to `cargo doc` as well as `cargo build`, which is what makes a broken
# intra-doc link a local build failure rather than a docs.rs-only surprise.
warnings = "deny"

# docs.rs sets `-D warnings` for itself and builds with the crate's default
# feature set, so a link that only resolves under a non-default feature fails
# there and nowhere else. `[package.metadata.docs.rs]` says all-features, and
# this says the same, so the local command and the published build agree.
[rustdoc]
all-features = true

# Convenience alias matching AGENTS.md so that `cargo l` reproduces the exact
# preflight profile documented in the task files. Keep this in sync with
# the preflight command in CLAUDE.md.
#
# The same profile is ALSO declared under [workspace.lints] in the root
# Cargo.toml, so a bare `cargo clippy` is equally strict. The duplication is
# deliberate: `cargo l` has to work on its own in a fresh checkout, and
# [workspace.lints] has to reach contributors who never use the alias. When a
# lint is added or relaxed, change both.
[alias]
l = "clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -W clippy::all -W clippy::pedantic -W clippy::nursery -W clippy::cargo -W clippy::perf -A clippy::module_name_repetitions -A clippy::must_use_candidate -A clippy::missing_errors_doc -A clippy::missing_panics_doc -A clippy::struct_excessive_bools -A clippy::multiple_crate_versions -D clippy::unwrap_used -D clippy::expect_used -D clippy::panic -D clippy::indexing_slicing -D clippy::cast_ptr_alignment -D clippy::suspicious -D warnings"
# Workspace maintenance tasks. `cargo xtask refresh-spec <version>` re-downloads
# a vendored MCP spec revision and updates the provenance manifest. Declared here
# so the task list's `cargo xtask ...` invocation works from a bare checkout.
xtask = "run --package xtask --"

--- pre-push ---
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Pre-push hook: the two CI checks that are cheap enough to run locally and
# that have caught real problems on this repository.
#
#   1. cargo fmt --all --check   — mirrors the `fmt` job in ci.yml exactly.
#   2. cargo audit               — the advisory scan, over every committed
#                                  lockfile, with the waivers from deny.toml.
#
# Why these two and not the rest of CI: the others (clippy, the test matrix,
# the conformance suite) take minutes. These take seconds. A hook that takes
# ten minutes is a hook people disable, and a disabled hook is worse than no
# hook, because it looks like a safety net.
#
# Why pre-push and not pre-commit: pre-commit runs before the commit is made,
# so a `cargo fmt` that rewrites files cannot be used there without silently
# amending what the author staged. Pre-push runs after the commit exists, so
# the check is a check — it reports, it does not rewrite. The fix is
# `cargo fmt --all && git commit --amend`, and the author stays in control of
# what lands in the history.
#
# The waivers are read from deny.toml rather than hardcoded here, because
# deny.toml is where the supply-chain policy already lives and a second list
# would drift from it. cargo audit has no config file of its own (0.22.2), so
# the list has to be passed on the command line; deny.toml is where it comes
# from.
#
# `--no-verify` bypasses this, as it bypasses every git hook. It is a guard
# against a habit, not a security boundary — CI runs the same checks and does
# not honour it.
set -uo pipefail

fix(schema): dispatch union arms on the member that tells them apart

Every generated wire union picked its arm by member order, which meant a
`tools/call` request decoded as an `InitializeRequest` and a 2026-07-28
server result landed in the generic `Result` arm. The misplacement was
silent: every generated type carries a `#[serde(flatten)]` catch-all, so
a value decoded into the wrong arm re-serialises to byte-identical JSON.

A union now dispatches two ways. Where the specification requires a
member of every alternative — `type` for content blocks, `method` for
requests and notifications — that member is read and an absent or unknown
value is a decode error rather than a guess. Where no such member
exists, the arm is chosen by the shape of the value: the arm's JSON kind,
the members it requires, and the properties two or more arms pin to
different values. The arm accounting for more of the value wins, and the
specification's own order breaks a tie.

A discriminator has to be *required* by every alternative, not merely
pinned by it. `ElicitRequestParams` pins `mode` to `form` and to `url`
but only the URL alternative requires it, so a form elicitation sent
without the tag is a value the specification accepts and a dispatcher
that insists on reading the tag would reject it.

The new `union_arm_selection` test covers all 112 unions across all six
revisions, building each alternative's value from the schema rather than
from a hand-written fixture, and asserts which arm was selected. Where
two alternatives produce byte-identical values, it asserts the weaker
invariant that still holds: the selected arm must be one that accepts
the value.

# is deliberately untracked by git, so this is a per-machine setting and never
# reaches a clone.
#

# opens, so the message does not exist yet. It can only check the staged tree.
# This rule is about the message, so it belongs here.
#
# Deletes and amends can bypass --no-verify here the same as anywhere else.
# This is a guard against a habit, not a security boundary.

message="$1"

if [ ! -f "$message" ]; then
    exit 0

feat(feature): cite every matrix row with the URL that documents it

AGENTS.md requires every row of the feature matrix to cite the spec
changelog section that introduced or removed it, and until now the
citations were prose: 32 rows named a revision, 12 named an SEP number,
and one named a URL. A reader could follow none of them to a document.

Every row now carries a `citation` — an https URL that names the
revision the row is attributed to — and the same URL appears in the doc
comment on the matching `Feature` variant, which is where a citation is
meant to be read. `2024-11-05` published no changelog at all, so its
rows cite the specification page directly; the two features whose
introducing changelog names no entry for them do the same.

A removal is cited like an addition: the row's citation still points at
the revision that introduced the feature, and the doc comment names the
revision and the changelog entry that removed it.

Three tests hold the matrix to that, and each says what it checks.
`every_row_cites_its_changelog` checks the citation is a URL naming the
row's revision. `every_variant_doc_comment_carries_its_citation` reads
this file back and checks the doc comment carries the row's URL.
`every_row_is_cited_and_ordered` keeps the ordering half. The last one
used to be the only test and its name over-promised; it now says what it
does, and the citation check has a name of its own.

checks the mapping, the generated one covers the values — and a test
asserts that the generated table's pairs are exactly the pairs the
vendored schemas define, so a table that silently lost a definition
cannot leave a hole nobody reports.

- **A test that asserts on `error.to_string()` asserts on the wrong
  string.** `anyhow`'s `Display` is the top context alone; the chain — the
  part that says *why* — is in `Debug` and in `{:#}`. The first version of
  the plain-HTTP refusal test failed because it read the top context and
  found "the provider's URL could not be used" instead of "is plain HTTP
  to `api.example.com`". A user sees the chain, so the test has to read
  the chain.


## Learnings: a union that cannot tell its arms apart (schema codegen)

The generated wire types dispatched their union arms on a hard-coded `type`
member. Where the specification pins `type` to distinct constants that works,
but most MCP unions pin something else, and the ones that pin nothing fell
back to `#[serde(untagged)]` — serde tries each member in declaration order
and keeps the first that round-trips. Every MCP request decoded into the
wrong arm (`tools/call` into `InitializeRequest`), and nothing reported it.

- **A catch-all member makes a wrong arm invisible.** Every generated type
  carries a `#[serde(flatten)]` for the members the schema does not name, so
  a value decoded into the wrong arm re-serialises to byte-identical JSON. A
  round-trip test passes for precisely the case it exists to catch. The
  assertion has to look at *which arm* was selected, not at the bytes.
- **A discriminator is only safe if the specification *requires* it.**
  `ElicitRequestParams` pins `mode` to `form` and to `url`, and both pin it
  in their own definition — but only the URL alternative *requires* it. A
  client that sends a form elicitation without the tag sends a value the
  specification accepts, and a dispatcher that insists on reading the tag
  rejects it. The rule that holds is "required by every alternative", not
  "pinned by every alternative".
- **The schema's own discriminator is not always the member that
  discriminates.** The order is `type`, `method`, `mode`, `resultType`, then
  anything else the members pin — and every alternative must pin it to a
  *distinct* value. A union whose members nest their own unions can have
  three members all tagged `string`, and no `match` on that can tell them
  apart however it is written.
- **Where no member discriminates, the shape does.** An arm is described by
  its JSON kind, the members it requires, the members it names, the shapes
  of those members, and the properties two or more arms pin to different
  values. The arm that accounts for more of the value wins; the
  specification's order breaks a tie. A constraint only one arm carries is
  that arm's own business and is not enforced by the dispatcher, because the
  generated type does not enforce it either.
- **Two alternatives can produce the same value, and then no dispatcher can
  separate them.** Four result alternatives differ only in members the schema
  does not require, so their canonical values are byte-identical. The test
  asserts the exact arm where the value is unambiguous and, where it is not,
  asserts the weaker invariant that still holds: the selected arm must be one
  that accepts the value. Asserting the exact arm there would be asserting
  something no implementation could provide.
- **The value has to be built from the schema.** Required members plus the
  members pinned to a constant, and nothing else. Adding an optional member
  makes the value look like a *different* alternative's value — `Result` and
  `SubscriptionsListenResult` both name `_meta`, and only the members one of
  them requires tell them apart. Building the value from the schema also
  means a revision that gains an alternative is covered without anyone
  remembering to add a case.
- **A schema-driven test needs the generator's own union list.** The Rust
  type name cannot be walked back to the schema, so the test carries the
  schema pointer for each union and the pointer has to resolve to an array.
  Two of the pointers did not resolve at first because a JSON pointer segment
  that names an index walks into an *array*, not an object.

## Learnings: a matrix row that cites nothing (feature catalogue)

The feature matrix had 39 rows and every one of them was a claim with no
document behind it. Thirty-two named a revision, twelve named an SEP number,
one named a URL, and none named a page a reader could open.

- **A citation has to be a URL, not a revision number.** "Introduced in
  2025-06-18" says when; it does not say where. The row now carries the
  changelog URL of the revision that introduced the feature, and the same URL
  appears in the doc comment on the matching `Feature` variant — which is
  where a citation is meant to be read, because that is where somebody
  looking up the feature will be.
- **A revision with no changelog cites its specification page.** 2024-11-05
  published no changelog at all, and two features (`toolAnnotations/
  lastModified` and `sampling/ context`) arrive in revisions whose changelog
  names no entry for them. A rule that every row must cite a changelog would
  have been a rule those rows cannot obey.
- **A removal is cited like an addition.** The row's citation still points at
  the revision that *introduced* the feature — the revision the feature belongs
  to for as long as it exists — and the doc comment names the revision and the
  changelog entry that removed it. Citing the removal instead would leave the
  row pointing at a document that does not describe the feature.
- **A test that reads the file back checks a different thing from a test that
  reads the table.** The table says the citation; the doc comment says where a
  reader will look. One without the other is a citation nobody reads when
  they are looking at the feature. The test that compares them parses this
  file's own source, so it fails when a doc comment loses its URL.
- **A test's name is a claim about what it checks.** The one test that
  existed checked the citation *and* the ordering *and* the table's coverage,
  and was called `every_row_is_cited_and_ordered`. Splitting it into three
  tests, each named for what it does, is what makes the suite readable
  months later.

## Learnings: the coverage that was not coverage (schema property suite)

The property suite proved the round trip for 62 of the 708
`(revision, definition)` pairs the vendored schemas define — 9%. The other
91% was not "less tested"; it was not tested at all, and a wire bug in any
of those types would have shipped.

- **A hand-written case list is a coverage hole waiting to happen.** The list
  was correct on the day it was written. A revision that gained a definition
  gained nothing in the list, and nothing reported the gap. The table is now
  generated by `build.rs` from the same schemas the values come from, so the
  list and the schemas cannot drift.
- **A generated table cannot check the mapping it derives.** The generated
  table names the type through the generator's own naming rule, so a rule
  that mapped `CallToolResult` onto `CallToolRequest` would produce a table
  that passes. The hand-written table stays because it names the type *by
  hand*, and that is what makes the definition-to-type mapping a
  compile-checked fact. The two halves are complementary: one checks the
  mapping, the other covers the values.
- **A generated table needs a test that checks the table.** `build.rs` could
  emit a table that silently lost a definition, and the hole would be exactly
  as invisible as the one the hand-written list had. The test compares the
  table's pairs against the pairs the vendored schemas define, as sets, so
  both a missing pair and a surplus one are reported.
- **The build script is a second copy of the schema model.** It parses each
  revision's `schema.json` to find the definitions, and the type path it
  writes is the generator's own mapping — so a definition that produced no
  type fails the test target's *compilation* rather than quietly skipping
  the round trip. A compile error is the right failure for a missing type.
- **A suite that cannot fail is not a suite.** Dropping
  `skip_serializing_if` from the generated optional fields — a `null` where
  the peer sent nothing — is caught by `draft/BooleanSchema`, which no
  hand-written case covered. The hand-written list caught the same mutation
  through `2025-03-26/AudioContent`, which is the same bug found twice; the
  generated table is what finds the ones nobody thought of.
- **The cost is a second `jsonschema` compilation per definition.** 553
  validators take about 1.8 s to compile and the whole suite 4.2 s to run.
  That is affordable, and the alternative — a hand-maintained list — costs
  correctness.

content.text:
All three issues are closed and the tree is clean. Here's where things landed.

## 1. Union arm dispatch — already done, now verified

`c22bfd84` (landed at the start of the session) replaced the fixed `type`-tag dispatcher. I checked the arm-level test's coverage against the generator's output: **112 union cases in the table, 112 unions emitted** (14/18/14/20/23/23 across the six revisions). The "5 of 65" figure in the issue is stale.

## 2. Feature matrix citations — `22cd58bf`

Every row now carries a `citation` URL and the **same URL appears in the `Feature` variant's doc comment**, which is where a reader looking up the feature will be. All 15 distinct URLs return 200. The SEP/PR prose comments were kept alongside.

`2024-11-05` published no changelog, so its rows cite the specification page; two features whose introducing changelog names no entry do the same. A removal cites the revision that *introduced* the feature, and the doc comment names the revision and entry that removed it.

Three tests, each named for what it checks — including one that reads `feature.rs` back and compares the doc comments against the table, since a citation that lives only in the table is a citation nobody reads.

## 3. Verification coverage — `fc097e9f`

**62 of 708 → 708 of 708** (9% → 100%). The table is now generated by `build.rs` from the same schemas the values come from, so a revision that gains a definition gains a case.

The hand-written 62-case table stays: it names the type *by hand*, which is what makes the definition→type **mapping** compile-checked. The generated table derives the path from the generator's own naming rule, so it can't check the mapping — it covers the **values**. A test asserts the generated pairs equal the pairs the schemas define, so the table can't silently lose one.

I mutation-tested it rather than trusting a green run: dropping `skip_serializing_if` from the generated optional fields is caught by `draft/BooleanSchema` — a definition no hand-written case covers. Suite cost: 771 tests, 5.0s.

## Also

`9b437d9b` — rustfmt for the ACP modules, which the pre-push hook's `cargo fmt --check` caught.

## One thing I found and left alone

[crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/naming.rs](/Users/ncampbell/Projects/rust/protocol-droid/crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/naming.rs) is **never compiled** — no `mod naming;` anywhere. It duplicates `emit.rs`'s naming logic, its `module_ident("draft")` returns `"v_draft"` where the live one returns `"draft"`, and its four doctests point at `protocol_droid_schema::adapters::primary::generator::naming::…`, a path that does not exist. Nothing catches any of that because the file is dead. Deleting it or wiring it in is a separate call from the three issues, so I didn't touch it.

I now have everything I need. Let me summarize the findings before acting:

**`naming.rs` is genuinely dead** — never compiled, never referenced, its `module_ident("draft")` → `"v_draft"` contradicts the live `"draft"`.

But deleting it alone would lose two things it had that the live code lacks. The live `field_ident` has **two real latent bugs** the dead file's tests would have caught:

input.message:
I found the dead file (`naming.rs`) has no live counterpart tests — and while checking, I found **two latent bugs in the live naming rule** that only the vendored schemas would trigger, not today's ones:

**Bug 1 — `field_ident` can emit an illegal Rust identifier.** `RESERVED` contains `self`/`Self`/`super`/`crate`, and the rule turns any reserved word into `r#name`. But `r#self`, `r#Self`, `r#super` and `r#crate` are **rejected by rustc** — only `self`/`Self`/`super`/`crate` are exempt from raw identifiers. A schema with a member named `self` would produce code that doesn't compile. No current schema has one, so it's latent.

**Bug 2 — `gen` is missing from `RESERVED`.** `gen` is a reserved keyword in edition 2024, and this crate is edition 2024. A member named `gen` would emit a bare `gen` field → compile error. The dead file's `RUST_KEYWORDS` *did* include `gen`; the live list dropped it.

Neither fires on the six vendored schemas today, so this is about the rule being wrong, not about a broken build.

How should I handle it?

def compiles(src):
    with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile('w', suffix='.rs', delete=False) as f:

    r = subprocess.run(['rustc','--edition','2024','--emit=metadata','-A','dead_code',p,'-o',p+'.meta'],

    if not ident: return False, "empty"
    if not (ident[0].isalpha() or ident[0]=='_'): return False, "leading digit/symbol"
    if ident in ("_","self","Self","super","crate"): return False, "reserved"
    if ident.startswith("r#"):

        return False, "bare keyword"
    return True, ""

STRICT = "as break const continue crate else enum extern false fn for if impl in let loop match mod move mut pub ref return self Self static struct super trait true type unsafe use where while async await dyn".split()
RESERVED_FUTURE = "abstract become box do final macro override priv typeof unsized virtual yield try gen".split()
ALL = STRICT + RESERVED_FUTURE
def compiles(src):
    with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile('w', suffix='.rs', delete=False) as f:
        f.write(src + "\n"); p=f.name
    r = subprocess.run(['rustc','--edition','2024','--crate-type=lib','--emit=metadata',p,'-o',p+'.meta'],capture_output=True)
    for q in (p,p+'.meta'):
        if os.path.exists(q): os.unlink(q)
    return r.returncode==0
no_raw, raw_ok = [], []
for w in ALL:
    if compiles(f"pub struct S {{ {w}: u8 }}"):
        no_raw.append(w)          # legal bare
    elif compiles(f"pub struct S {{ r#{w}: u8 }}"):
        raw_ok.append(w)          # legal only as raw
    else:
        print("NEITHER BARE NOR RAW WORKS:", w)
print("cannot be bare, must be raw:", sorted(raw_ok))
print("legal bare (so r# is only a style choice):", sorted(no_raw))

# Primer — protocol-droid schema generator cleanup

Session: `00ecf7f2-acba-4582-a148-8d4c26efc71b`
Repo: `/Users/ncampbell/Projects/rust/protocol-droid` (branch unknown — check `git status`)
Written: end of segment, work paused mid-flight at the user's request.

---

## 1. Where the work came from

An earlier review of the schema generator raised three gaps:

1. **Union discrimination is hard-coded.** The generator dispatches union arms on a
   fixed `type` property. The reviewer's point: the discriminator should be
   *discovered* — look for a property common to every member whose value is a
   distinct `const`. Where no member pins a const (2026-07-28's `resultType` is
   free-form), the untagged fallback is unsafe unless the generic `Result` member
   sorts most-specific-first, or the build fails rather than emitting a union
   that silently mis-assigns.
2. **Feature-matrix citations.** 39 variants: 32 cite a revision, 12 an SEP number,
   **1 a URL**. `AGENTS.md` requires "a doc comment with the URL".
   `every_row_is_cited_and_ordered` (`domain/mcp/feature.rs:1184`) only checks the
   revision is known and ordered — the name over-promises.
3. **Verification coverage was 9%.** The property suite covered 62 of 708
   (revision, definition) pairs; the arm-level test covered 5 of 65 tagged unions.

**Gaps 2 and 3 are DONE** (see the commit list in §2). Gap 1 was partially addressed
by `c22bfd84` (tag dispatch), and the *residual* bug class it documents turned out
to be the naming layer, which is what this segment is about.

## 2. Commits already landed (relevant, recent)

```
fc097e9f test(schema): round-trip every definition of every revision   <- closes gap 3
22cd58bf feat(feature): cite every matrix row with the URL that documents it  <- closes gap 2
c22bfd84 fix(schema): dispatch union arms on the member that tells them apart  <- gap 1, partial
9b437d9b style: apply rustfmt to the ACP modules
```

So the *naming* work below is a cleanup that fell out of gap 1's aftermath, not a
gap-1 deliverable.

## 3. What this segment actually did

### 3.1 Deleted dead code

`crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/naming.rs` (305 lines) — **deleted, staged**.

It was a *parallel* naming implementation: its own `RUST_KEYWORDS` list, its own
`words()` / `push_camel_words()` / `field_ident()`, and its own `#[cfg(test)] mod tests`.
It had **zero callers** — `generator/mod.rs` declares only `pub mod emit;` and
`pub mod schema_model;`. It survived in the tree because `build.rs` `#[path]`-includes
`emit.rs` and `schema_model.rs`, so the file compiled without ever being wired to
anything.

Its naming rules had *drifted* from the live ones in `emit.rs` (it used the
trailing-underscore convention universally; the live code uses `r#` for keywords).
Two live bugs were hiding behind the dead file:

### 3.2 Bug #1 — `r#self` / `r#super` / `r#crate` are compile errors

**The dead branch.** The original `field_ident` was:

```rust
if RESERVED.iter().any(|r| *r == snake) {
    format!("r#{snake}")          // <-- fires for "self"/"super"/"crate"
} else if is_keyword(&snake) {
    format!("{snake}_")           // <-- UNREACHABLE
}
```

`is_keyword(name)` is `RESERVED.contains(&name)` — the *same predicate* as the first
branch. The `else if` could never run, so the trailing-underscore fallback existed in
source but never executed. Every keyword therefore became `r#word`, and four of those
are not legal Rust:

> rustc rejects raw-identifier syntax for exactly four words: `self`, `Self`, `super`,
> `crate`. `r#self` is not an identifier. Neither is bare `self` as a field name.

**The fix** (`emit.rs`, `field_ident`): check a new `NOT_RAW_IDENTIFIABLE` list
*first* → `{snake}_`; then `RESERVED` → `r#{snake}`; then the pre-existing
leading-underscore trim; else bare `snake`.

```rust
const NOT_RAW_IDENTIFIABLE: &[&str] = &["self", "super", "crate"];
```

The list is matched against the *lowercased snake* form, so a member named `Self`
arrives as `self` and is covered by that one entry — no separate `"Self"` needed.

### 3.3 Bug #2 — `gen` was missing from `RESERVED`

Rust 2024 (this crate's edition) reserves `gen`. It is *not* a strict keyword, but it
cannot be used as an identifier at all: `type gen = u8;` and `struct gen;` both fail to
compile in edition 2024, while `type gen_ = u8;` compiles. The old `RESERVED` list had
no `gen`, so a schema member named `gen` would have emitted a bare `gen` field.

**The fix:** added `"gen"` to `RESERVED`. It now maps to `r#gen` (which *is* legal —
verified).

Note: `union` was already in `RESERVED` and is not actually reserved in 2024. It was
left in place deliberately — a plausible MCP member name, and reserving it costs
nothing. The doc comment on `RESERVED` now says so explicitly.

### 3.4 Verification sweep (all rustc/clippy-verified, not eyeballed)

- rustc keyword matrix: exactly 4 words (`crate`, `self`, `Self`, `super`) are neither
  bare-legal nor raw-legal; every other reserved word works as `r#word`.
- `r#union`, `r#typeof`, `r#become`, `r#gen`, `r#try`, `r#box` all compile.
- Real clippy run on candidate identifiers: `pub _meta: u8` trips
  `clippy::pub_underscore_fields` — this confirms the existing leading-underscore
  trim in `field_ident` is load-bearing, not decoration. `pub self_`, `pub super_`,
  `pub crate_`, `pub n2fa`, `pub field`, `pub r#union` are all clean.
- serde round-trip: `#[serde(rename = "")]` and `#[serde(rename = "2fa")]` both
  serialize/deserialize correctly — so the emitter's rename mechanism makes any
  identifier transform wire-safe.
- **All property names across all six vendored revisions**: 136 distinct at
  definition level, 157 counting nested inline objects. Only 6 are problematic:
  `$schema` (leading-underscore), `_meta` (leading-underscore), and
  `const`/`enum`/`ref`/`type` (keywords). All handled by the existing rules.
- **All 192 definition names** against the keyword set: **zero** collisions.
- **Per-definition field-identifier collisions** across every definition of every
  revision: **zero** collisions.

### 3.5 Current working-tree state

```
M crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/emit.rs      (unstaged)
D crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/naming.rs     (staged)
```

`emit.rs` diff is +26/−6. The build passes:

```
$ RUSTC_WRAPPER= SCCACHE_DISABLE=1 cargo build --workspace --all-features
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 26.62s
```

## 4. What is NOT done

1. **Regression tests** — the main remaining deliverable. Details in §6.
2. **`.papertowel.toml` stale reference** — line 108 still points at the deleted file:
   ```
   # crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/naming.rs is about the conversion
   ```
   That comment is a lint-rationale note explaining why the word "underscores" survives
   the project's own word ban. The file it cites no longer exists; the note should be
   repointed at `crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/emit.rs` (which is where
   the JSON-name → Rust-identifier conversion actually lives now).
3. **Full preflight** — not yet run.
4. **Commit** — nothing committed yet; the deletion is staged but uncommitted.
5. **`PROGRESS.md`** — not updated. This work does not map to a numbered task in
   `tasks/` (T12–T31 are all unrelated protocol work); it is a review-driven cleanup.
   A line in the "Accumulated Learnings" section would be appropriate.

## 5. Key file map

| Path | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| `crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/emit.rs` | The live naming implementation. **Modified.** 1566 lines. Key symbols: `module_ident` (1449), `type_ident` (1463), `field_ident` (1491), `to_snake` (1510), `variant_ident` (1527), `RESERVED` (1546), `NOT_RAW_IDENTIFIABLE` (1562), `is_keyword` (1564). |
| `crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/naming.rs` | **DELETED.** The dead file. Its test module held cases worth porting: casing splits, `field_ident("2fa") == "_2fa"`, `module_ident("draft") == "draft"`, and an MCP property-set collision check. |
| `crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/mod.rs` | 29 lines; declares only `emit` and `schema_model` as `pub mod`. |
| `crates/protocol-droid-schema/build.rs` | `#[path]`-includes `emit.rs` + `schema_model.rs`; calls `emit::module_ident` (line ~223) and `emit::type_ident` (~291). **Consequence:** `emit.rs` must stay free of `crate::` references and may only use crates in `[build-dependencies]`. |
| `crates/protocol-droid-schema/tests/generation.rs` | The generator integration test, 262 lines. `REVISIONS` const at line 24: `("2024-11-05", 79)`, `("2025-03-26", 83)`, `("2025-06-18", 91)`, `("2025-11-25", 145)`, `("2026-07-28", 155)`, `("draft", 155)`. Has `fail(message) -> !` helper (line 82) using `std::process::exit(1)` because `panic!` is denied. |
| `crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/domain/manifest.rs` | Precedent for a `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` block *inside* a `#[path]`-included file (line ~735+). Its module carries a pre-existing `#![expect(clippy::expect_used, reason = "...")]` at line 742. |
| `crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/schema_model.rs` | Parsed schema model: `SchemaFile`, `Schema` with `properties: BTreeMap<String, Box<Self>>`, `required`, `union`, `intersect`. |
| `crates/protocol-droid-schema/Cargo.toml` | `default = ["codegen"]`, `codegen = []`. Dev-deps: `proptest`, `jsonschema`, `assert_matches`. |

## 6. The remaining work, in detail

### 6.1 Regression tests — placement decision

Two options:

- **`tests/generation.rs`** (integration). Lower risk. `emit::field_ident` is `pub`, and
  the file already imports `protocol_droid_schema::generator::emit`. But: the file
  loads real vendored schemas; testing `field_ident("self")` needs no schema at all.
- **`#[cfg(test)] mod tests` inside `emit.rs`**. Precedented by `manifest.rs`. Tests
  the function where it lives, which is where a future edit will look. Caveat: the
  library's `generator` module is behind `#[cfg(feature = "codegen")]`, so these tests
  only run with `--all-features` — which `cargo l` and CI both use, and `cargo test
  --workspace --all-features` (the project preflight) uses.

**Recommendation: a `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` in `emit.rs`.** `field_ident` is a pure
function with no schema dependency, and the tests belong next to the rules they pin.
Gate it with `#[cfg(all(test, feature = "codegen"))]` if the library-side compile
needs it — verify by running both `cargo test -p protocol-droid-schema` (default
features, codegen on) and `cargo test -p protocol-droid-schema --no-default-features`.

Note the `#[path]`-include interaction: `emit.rs` is compiled into `build.rs` too, but
`build.rs` is never compiled in test mode, so `#[cfg(test)]` content is excluded there.
`manifest.rs` establishes the precedent — follow it exactly.

### 6.2 Regression tests — what to assert

Minimum set:

```rust
// The four raw-rejected words take a trailing underscore, never r#.
assert_eq!(field_ident("self"),  "self_");
assert_eq!(field_ident("super"), "super_");
assert_eq!(field_ident("crate"), "crate_");
assert_eq!(field_ident("Self"),  "self_");   // snake-cased to "self"

// The 2024 reserved word.
assert_eq!(field_ident("gen"), "r#gen");     // never bare "gen"

// The pre-existing raw-identifier path still works — PIN IT.
assert_eq!(field_ident("type"), "r#type");
```

Plus two property-style tests over the real vendored data:

- **Collision test:** for every definition of every revision, collect
  `field_ident(name)` over its properties; assert no two members of one definition
  collapse to the same Rust identifier. (Already verified manually: zero collisions
  under the new rules — the test pins it.)
- **Legality test:** assert every emitted identifier is a legal Rust identifier
  (bare or raw), and that no `RESERVED` word maps to a bare identifier and no
  `NOT_RAW_IDENTIFIABLE` word maps to a raw identifier.

`assert_matches!` / `debug_assert_matches!` are available (dev-dep `assert_matches` is
present, and both are stabilized) and print `Debug` on failure — prefer them over
`assert!(matches!(..))`.

### 6.3 Hard constraints on the test code

From `AGENTS.md` (non-negotiable, and `cargo l` enforces them across `--all-targets`):

- **No `.unwrap()`, `.expect()`, `.expect_err()`, `panic!()`.** Return
  `Result<(), E>` from the test and use `?`. When fallible calls answer unrelated
  error types, collect them in a small `enum Failure` with a `From` impl each (see
  `engine.rs` and `registry.rs` for the pattern).
- **No index slicing** — `&vec[i]`, `&s[0..n]`, `arr[0]`, `s[..n]`. Use `.get(i)` with
  explicit handling, or `slice.first()`, or `let [first, ..] = slice else { .. }`.
  `clippy::indexing_slicing` does **not** fire on a constant index into a fixed-size
  array (`cases[0]` on `[(..); N]` passes clean) — that is exactly the case a test
  reaches for, so the lint will not catch it for you. **Iterate instead.**
- **Do NOT add `#[expect(clippy::unwrap_used, ...)]` to a new test module.** The
  attribute only grandfathered code that predates the rule; adding one to a new test
  is how the rule gets skipped wholesale rather than obeyed.
- `#[allow(clippy::...)]` is forbidden outright. `#[expect(..., reason = "...")]` is
  allowed with a reason.
- Prefer `.is_multiple_of(n)` over `% n == 0`.
- Doc comments on public items need `# Examples` / `# Errors` / `# Panics` sections
  where the function can fail in those ways.

## 7. Preflight (must pass before commit)

Run from the **repo root** (the toolchain pin lives there — a bare `cargo clippy` run
in `/tmp` used a different, 1.99.0 toolchain):

```bash
cargo fmt --all --check && cargo build --workspace --all-features && \
  cargo test --workspace --all-features && cargo l && cargo deny --all-features check
```

`cargo l` is the alias from `.cargo/config.toml`:
`-W clippy::all -W clippy::pedantic -W clippy::nursery -W clippy::cargo -W clippy::perf`,
with `module_name_repetitions`, `must_use_candidate`, `missing_errors_doc`,
`missing_panics_doc`, `struct_excessive_bools`, `multiple_crate_versions` allowed;
`unwrap_used`, `expect_used`, `panic`, `indexing_slicing`, `cast_ptr_alignment`,
`suspicious` denied; `-D warnings` last.

`cargo deny` reads a **cached** advisory DB locally. A green local pass can still be
missing an advisory CI will fail on. Do not narrow an `ignore` in `deny.toml` without
re-running `cargo deny --all-features check` **with network access**.

Toolchain: pinned to **1.98.1** (`rust-toolchain.toml`), verified
`rustc 1.98.1 (48a229cea 2026-09-01)` / `clippy 0.1.98`. Never pin 1.97.0 (LLVM
miscompilation, rust-lang/rust#159035). `rust-version = "1.98"` in
`[workspace.package]`.

## 8. Commit

Conventional commits, e.g.:

```
fix(schema): escape the four keywords rustc refuses as raw identifiers
```

with the trailer:

```
Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>
```

Do not force-add files ignored by `.gitignore`. Never do in-place shell rewrites like
`printf '%s' "$(cat f)" > f` — use edit tools and verify with `git diff --stat`.

## 9. Facts worth not re-deriving

- **Raw identifiers work for every reserved word except `self`, `Self`, `super`,
  `crate`.** Verified with rustc, edition 2024. Everything else → `r#word`.
- **`gen` is reserved in Rust 2024** but is not a strict keyword. Cannot be an
  identifier in any form; `gen_` and `r#gen` are both legal.
- **`is_keyword(name)` is `RESERVED.contains(&name)`** — the identical predicate to
  `RESERVED.iter().any(|r| *r == name)`. That redundancy is what made the
  trailing-underscore branch in `field_ident` unreachable. Watch for it when editing.
- **`to_snake` does not strip a leading underscore** — hence `field_ident`'s separate
  leading-underscore branch.
- **`field_ident`'s output is always wire-safe** because the emitter writes
  `#[serde(rename = "{prop_name}")]` whenever the field name differs from the
  property name (`emit.rs` ~line 1185). Serde handles empty-string and numeric
  renames correctly (round-trip verified).
- **`clippy::pub_underscore_fields` (pedantic) fires on `pub _meta`.** Any fallback
  identifier must not start with `_`.
- **`type_ident` uses the trailing-underscore convention** (via `is_keyword` → push
  `'_'`), because `Self_` / `crate_` are legal *type* names. `field_ident` needs the
  `r#`/underscore *split* because it handles *field* names. Do not unify them.
- **`module_ident("draft") == "draft"`**; other revisions → `v2025_11_25` style.
- **`build.rs` `#[path]`-includes shared sources**, so those files may not reference
  `crate::` and may only use `[build-dependencies]` crates.
- The deleted `naming.rs` used `field_ident("2fa") == "_2fa"` (leading underscore kept,
  unlike the live code which trims it). The live behaviour is the trimmed one —
  `2fa` → `n2fa`? No: `to_snake("2fa")` → `"2fa"`, and `2fa` does not start with `_`,
  so the live result is `"2fa"`. **Verify before porting any case from the dead file.**

### 3.2b Bug #3 (found late, during primer verification) — digit-leading member names

**Not yet fixed.** Found while verifying the primer's claims; recording it here because
it is the same bug class and it is *not* covered by the two fixes above.

`field_ident` output is used directly as the Rust field name (`emit.rs:1184-1199`
writes `pub {field}: {ty}`), and `to_snake` does **not** guard a leading digit:

```
to_snake("2fa")    -> "2fa"
field_ident("2fa") -> "2fa"      // ILLEGAL — `pub 2fa: u8` does not compile
```

Verified with rustc, edition 2024:

```
error: expected identifier, found `2fa`
help: identifiers cannot start with a number
```

`pub _2fa: u8` compiles fine. Note the asymmetry: `type_ident` *does* guard this
(`if i == 0 && ch.is_ascii_digit() { out.push('_') }`, `emit.rs:1467-1470`) — only the
*field* path is unguarded.

**Why the dead file mattered here.** `naming.rs`'s `field_ident` produced `_2fa`
(trailing-underscore convention with a leading-underscore guard). The live
implementation regressed to bare `2fa`. So deleting the dead file did not cause this,
but the dead file was the only place the case was handled — and it had a test for it
(`field_ident("2fa") == "_2fa"`).

**Current blast radius: zero.** Scanned all six vendored revisions for property names
beginning with a digit: **NONE**. So this cannot bite today. It would bite the first
time upstream ships a member like `"2fa"` — and the failure is a *build* failure in
the generated crate, not a runtime one, so it would be caught immediately rather than
silently. Still worth fixing, because the whole point of this segment was to make the
identifier rules provably correct rather than accidentally correct.

**Suggested fix** (mirrors `type_ident`, and keeps `#[serde(rename)]` doing the wire
work — the emitter already writes `#[serde(rename = "{prop_name}")]` whenever
`field != *prop_name`):

```rust
} else if snake.starts_with(|c: char| c.is_ascii_digit()) {
    // A member name may start with a digit — upstream's `"2fa"` does. Rust
    // identifiers may not, so the field gains a leading underscore and keeps
    // the serde rename back to the wire name.
    format!("_{snake}")
}
```

Order matters: this check must come **before** the leading-underscore-trim branch
(which would otherwise strip the very underscore that makes it legal), and after the
`RESERVED` / `NOT_RAW_IDENTIFIABLE` branches.

# Changelog

All notable changes to `protocol-droid` are recorded here. The format follows
[Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/), and the project
adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html).

Every entry cites the commit that made the change, so a claim here can be
checked against the code rather than taken on the changelog's word.

## [Unreleased]

### Changed

- **The cross-protocol bridge is two protocol adapters and one composition,
  not a hand-written translator for every pair of protocols.** (`2289b30c`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/protocol_adapter.rs`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/mcp_adapter.rs`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/a2a_adapter.rs`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/composed.rs`) The MCP ↔ A2A
  translation was a pair of functions that knew both vocabularies — one that
  turned `SendMessage` into `tools/call`, one that turned it back. A third
  protocol would have needed two more, and the pair nobody wrote about would
  have been the pair nobody tested.

  The translation now lives in per-protocol adapters behind a
  `ProtocolAdapter` seam, and `ComposedCodec` puts two of them together:
  lift on the way out, lower on the way back, with the IR in between. An
  adapter knows one protocol and does not mention the other, so a bridge
  between two protocols nobody wrote a translator for works the same way as
  the one that was.

  The IR gained the types the adapters meet at — `IrCall`, `IrMethod` and
  `IrOutcome` at `crates/protocol-droid/src/domain/ir/call.rs` — and a loss
  that has no counterpart on the other side is now recorded in the
  translation report rather than dropped in silence: an A2A part with no MCP
  counterpart, a task's artifacts, and structured content with no A2A
  counterpart are all reported.

  `CrossBridgePeer::new` lost its `downstream_side` parameter. The codec is
  built from a downstream adapter and an upstream adapter, so it knows which
  side it is; a caller that passed the side separately could disagree with
  the codec, and the disagreement would have shown up as a method the bridge
  refused for no visible reason.

### Fixed

- **The A2A leg of the bridge sent the agent arguments it could not read.**
  (`2289b30c`,

## [Unreleased]

### Changed

- **The cross-protocol bridge is two protocol adapters and one composition,
  not a hand-written translator for every pair of protocols.** (`2289b30c`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/protocol_adapter.rs`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/mcp_adapter.rs`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/a2a_adapter.rs`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/composed.rs`) The MCP ↔ A2A
  translation was a pair of functions that knew both vocabularies — one that
  turned `SendMessage` into `tools/call`, one that turned it back. A third
  protocol would have needed two more, and the pair nobody wrote about would
  have been the pair nobody tested.

  The translation now lives in per-protocol adapters behind a
  `ProtocolAdapter` seam, and `ComposedCodec` puts two of them together:
  lift on the way out, lower on the way back, with the IR in between. An
  adapter knows one protocol and does not mention the other, so a bridge
  between two protocols nobody wrote a translator for works the same way as
  the one that was.

  The IR gained the types the adapters meet at — `IrCall`, `IrMethod` and
  `IrOutcome` at `crates/protocol-droid/src/domain/ir/call.rs` — and a loss
  that has no counterpart on the other side is now recorded in the
  translation report rather than dropped in silence: an A2A part with no MCP
  counterpart, a task's artifacts, and structured content with no A2A
  counterpart are all reported.

  `CrossBridgePeer::new` lost its `downstream_side` parameter. The codec is
  built from a downstream adapter and an upstream adapter, so it knows which
  side it is; a caller that passed the side separately could disagree with
  the codec, and the disagreement would have shown up as a method the bridge
  refused for no visible reason.

## Past advisories

None. The repository's first release was tagged after the
SECURITY-REVIEW audit in October 2026, and no vulnerability
has been reported against a tagged release.

## Dependency advisories in the published graph

A dependency advisory is not an advisory against this crate, but it is
still something a consumer of a published version inherits, so it is
recorded here.

**RUSTSEC-2026-0385 — `ctutils` — affected every published version up
to and including 0.5.2. Fixed in 0.5.3.**

`ctutils 0.4.3`'s `Choice` mask generation could compile to a branch
on secret values, and its `u128` comparisons were not constant-time on
32-bit targets. Upstream fixed it in `ctutils 0.4.4`.

The path into this crate is `protocol-droid` → `hmac 0.13` → `digest
0.11.3` → `ctutils`, and `ctutils` is pulled in by `digest`'s `mac`
feature rather than by `hmac`'s own use of it: `digest/src/mac.rs` does
`use ctutils::CtEq;` and calls `ct_eq(tag)` to compare a MAC tag. The
reachable path is this crate's own HMAC comparison in
`application/mcp/input_required.rs`, where `StateKey::open` verifies a
`requestState` MAC with `verify_slice`. That is a real comparison over a
value derived from a server-held key, so the regression is a genuine
defect and not a theoretical one.

What a consumer needs to know:

- **A library consumer** resolves their own dependency graph, so a
  fresh resolve picks up a patched `ctutils` on its own. A consumer
  whose own lockfile still pins `ctutils 0.4.3` should run
  `cargo update -p ctutils`; the requirement is `^0.4`, so the patched
  version is already permitted.
- **A binary consumer** of `protocol-droid-cli` is the case that needs
  attention. A binary crate publishes its `Cargo.lock`, and `cargo
  install` honours it, so `cargo install protocol-droid-cli --version
  0.5.2` installed a binary built against `ctutils 0.4.3`. 0.5.3 ships
  the patched version, as does every release since.

The advisory was published on 2026-10-23, after 0.5.2 was tagged on
2026-10-22, so the fix could not have shipped in 0.5.2.

**RUSTSEC-2026-0387 — `crypto-bigint` — waived, not fixed.**

`crypto-bigint 0.5.5` has a constant-time regression in its `u128`
operations. It is reached through `jsonwebtoken`'s `rust_crypto`
backend → `p256`/`p384` → `ecdsa` → `elliptic-curve`, and no upgrade
path exists: the fix sits behind `p256`/`p384 0.14`, which
`jsonwebtoken 11.1.0`'s caret requirements do not admit.

It is unreachable from this code. The only path to `elliptic-curve` is
ECDSA *verification*, which runs on the public key, the message hash
and the signature's own `r` and `s` — no secret scalar reaches the
affected operations. The signing path is the reachable one and this
crate has no path to it: `jsonwebtoken`'s `EllipticCurveKeyParameters`
carries only `kty`, `crv`, `x` and `y`, so a JWK has no field in which
to carry a private scalar.

The waiver and its full reasoning live in
[`deny.toml`](https://github.com/greysquirr3l/protocol-droid/blob/main/deny.toml),
which is the single list of accepted advisories. It should be re-read
whenever `jsonwebtoken` or `rsa` changes, not waited on a schedule.

## Acknowledgements

The threat model and the no-finding summary draw on the
[OWASP Top 10:2025](https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/) and
[OWASP API Security Top 10:2023](https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0x11-t10/)
checklists. The MCP-spec-specific surface is read against the
official [Model Context Protocol specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/)

  current `protocol-droid` version.** The three excluded from the workspace
  (`fuzz`, `interop_rmcp`, `interop_ts_sdk`) had drifted: the root lockfile
  moved to `ctutils 0.4.5` and the interop fixture's did not, so it kept the
  vulnerable `0.4.3` until the pre-push hook blocked the push. The other two
  were staler still, pinning `protocol-droid 0.1.0` against a workspace at
  0.5.2.

  All four are current now, and each records `ctutils 0.4.5`. The hook scans
  every committed lockfile, so this is the state it was already asking for;
  the drift was that nobody had run it since the advisory landed. The CI gap
  this exposes is recorded in `SECURITY.md` rather than closed here.

- **`RUSTSEC-2026-0387` on `crypto-bigint 0.5.5` is waived, with the
  argument written down.** (`deny.toml`) It is reached through
  `jsonwebtoken`'s `rust_crypto` backend → `p256`/`p384` → `ecdsa` →
  `elliptic-curve`, and there is no upgrade path: the fix sits behind
  `p256`/`p384 0.14`, which `jsonwebtoken 11.1.0`'s caret requirements
  (`^0.13.2` / `^0.13.0`) do not admit, and 11.1.0 is the latest release
  whose `master` carries the same pins.

  It is unreachable because the only path to `elliptic-curve` here is ECDSA
  *verification*. `ecdsa`'s `verify_prehashed` runs on the public key, the
  message hash and the signature's own `r` and `s` — no secret scalar
  reaches the affected operations. The signing path (`sign_prehashed`, which
  calls `k.invert()` on a secret scalar) is the reachable one and this crate
  has no path to it: `jsonwebtoken`'s `EllipticCurveKeyParameters` carries
  only `kty`, `crv`, `x` and `y`, so a JWK has no field in which to carry a
  private scalar.

  The waiver carries that argument in full, so the next person to read
  `deny.toml` does not have to re-derive it.

- **`enforce_admins` is on.** (`.github/branch-protection.json`) It was
  `false`, which meant a repository admin could push straight to `main` and
  bypass the pull-request requirement. Enabling Dependabot's alerts made this
  worth closing: an advisory is now reported against the repository, and the
  person who would fix it could also skip the review saying the fix is right.

  The release chain is unaffected — Auto Tag pushes a tag, and branch

- **`ip-address` in the interop fixture is fixed rather than suppressed.**

## How a vulnerability gets found

A report is the best route and not the only one. Three things run without
anyone looking:

| Where | What it checks | Coverage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `supply chain` CI job | `cargo deny` against a freshly fetched advisory database | all four committed lockfiles |
| Dependabot alerts | advisory database against every manifest | root, `site/`, and the interop fixture |
| Secret scanning | credential patterns across the history and every push | whole repository |
| `pre-push` hook | `cargo audit` over every committed lockfile | all four, including the three outside the workspace |

Two gaps are worth stating plainly rather than leaving to be discovered:

**Every committed lockfile now gets a CI-side advisory watch.** Until the
`supply chain` job was extended, it scanned the root lockfile only.
`crates/protocol-droid/fuzz/`, `crates/protocol-droid/tests/interop_rmcp/`
and `crates/protocol-droid/tests/interop_ts_sdk/` are excluded from the
workspace, so `cargo deny` never saw their dependency graphs; the pre-push
hook covered them locally, which is a mitigation, not equivalent coverage.

The job now scans all four, one step per lockfile, and each of those
steps passes `--locked`. Without `--locked`, `cargo metadata` re-resolves
the graph and rewrites the lockfile on disk, so the scan would report on
a dependency set nobody committed — a different check, not a stricter
one. With `--locked`, the scan reports on the lockfile as committed, and
fails loudly when that lockfile is stale.

That gap was not theoretical. When `ctutils` was bumped to 0.4.5 for
RUSTSEC-2026-0385, the root `Cargo.lock` was updated and the interop
fixture's was not, so the fixture kept `ctutils 0.4.3` until the pre-push
hook blocked the push. The hook was the only thing that saw it, and the
lockfile it caught was stale on more than the advisory: it still pinned
`protocol-droid 0.1.0` against a workspace at 0.5.2.

The `interop_ts_sdk` fixture is the one case where a manifest *is* watched:
Dependabot's security updates reach it, and it is declared in
`dependabot.yml` so a transitive advisory gets a bump proposal rather than
sitting unnoticed. Note that `npm install` honours the committed lockfile,
so it will not self-heal — the lockfile has to be updated on purpose. The
other two are Rust, and are now covered by CI as well as by the hook.

**The site is built in CI, but the peer-range gap is still worth knowing.**
The `site` job installs with `--frozen-lockfile`, runs `astro check` and
`astro build`, and asserts the output has the expected shape, so a change
under `site/` that does not build fails the PR rather than passing every
check. It was not always so: Dependabot's astro 5 → 7 PR passed fourteen green
Rust checks without building, because starlight 0.30 pins `astro: ^5.0.0` and
`pnpm install` does not enforce peer ranges — the failure appears only at
build time. `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` does not change that; it
enforces the *lockfile*, not the peer ranges.

`deny.toml` is the single list of accepted advisories, and it is the same
list the `pre-push` hook reads. A waiver belongs there with a reason saying
why the advisory is unreachable from this code; there is no second place to
record one.

## What is out of scope

- **The consumer's deployment.** A consumer that disables TLS
  verification on its own `reqwest` client, that does not set
  `Content-Security-Policy` on its own HTTP server, that picks
  a token-storage adapter that is not `OsSecrets` and stores
  the token in a world-readable file — that is the consumer's
  deployment, not this library.
- **A2A peers that are not under the consumer's control.** A
  push-notification webhook URL that resolves to a private
  network is refused by the SSRF denylist at config time, and
  re-validated at delivery time. A URL that resolves to a
  public network the consumer did not intend to send to is a
  consumer-configuration problem.
- **A peer that has compromised the consumer's process.** The
  library's parsers are fuzzed against malicious input; a peer
  that already has code execution on the consumer's host is
  not in the threat model.
- **MCP revisions older than the lowest vendored one.** The
  library does not claim to speak revisions it does not have
  wire types for. A consumer who needs revision `X` and
  `X` is not in `crates/protocol-droid-schema/spec/` is not
  in scope.
- **The CLI's own configuration file format.** The CLI is a
  thin adapter; the configuration it parses is the consumer's
  to validate, and a bad config is the consumer's error, not
  a security issue.

## Response timeline

| Step                                        | Window          |
| ------------------------------------------- | --------------- |
| Initial acknowledgement                     | 7 days          |
| Triage and impact assessment                | 30 days         |
| Patch landed (or status update)             | 60 days         |
| Public advisory and CVE request (if needed) | 90 days         |
| Embargoed release at the consumer's request | by request      |

A "status update" in the 60-day row is a maintainer message in
the original advisory thread explaining what is blocking and
what the next step is — a patch that needs a contract change,
a reproducer that does not reproduce, a CVE that is still in
the CNA queue. The status update is what prevents a silent
60-day pause.

`CrossBridgePeer::new` lost its `downstream_side` parameter. The codec is
  built from a downstream adapter and an upstream adapter, so it knows which
  side it is; a caller that passed the side separately could disagree with
  the codec, and the disagreement would have shown up as a method the bridge
  refused for no visible reason.

### Fixed

- **The A2A leg of the bridge sent the agent arguments it could not read.**
  (`2289b30c`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/a2a_adapter.rs`) An MCP
  `tools/call` carried `arguments` as an object, and the bridge put it on the
  A2A wire inside a data part as `{"data": {"data": {…}}}`. The agent read
  the call's arguments out of the nested object rather than the object
  itself, so a tool that expected `{"query": "weather"}` was handed
  `{"data": {"query": "weather"}}`.

- **The A2A leg of the bridge wrote a `kind` key the spec does not name.**
  (`2289b30c`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/a2a_adapter.rs`) A part was
  written as `{"kind": "data", "data": {…}}`. The spec's part shape is the
  proto's `oneof content`: the object has exactly one of `text`, `file` or
  `data` as a top-level field, with no discriminator. That is what the
  crate's own A2A server sends, what the A2A conformance fixtures expect,
  and what the vendored `a2a.proto` describes — so the bridge was speaking
  a dialect of A2A that the rest of the crate does not speak.

- **A generated union picked its arm by member order.** (`c22bfd84`,
  `crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/emit.rs`) A `tools/call`
  request decoded as an `InitializeRequest`, and a `2026-07-28` result landed
  in the generic `Result` arm. Nothing showed it: every generated type
  carries a flattened catch-all, so a value in the wrong arm re-serialises to
  byte-identical JSON. A union now reads the member the specification
  requires of every alternative — `type`, `method` — and an absent or
  unknown value is a decode error. Where no such member exists the arm is
  chosen by the value's shape, and the specification's order breaks a tie.

- **A schema member named `self`, `super` or `crate` generated a field that
  did not compile.** (`09732f65`,
  `crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/emit.rs`) `field_ident` tried
  the raw-identifier branch first and the trailing-underscore branch second,
  on the same predicate, so the second could never run and `self` came out as
  `r#self`, which rustc rejects. The three now take a trailing underscore,
  `gen` is reserved for edition 2024, and a member that starts with a digit
  gains a leading underscore. No vendored schema has such a member today; the
  next upstream one would have broken the build. An unreferenced 305-line
  `naming.rs` carrying a second, drifted copy of these rules is gone.

- **A bridge session's inbound queue grew without limit, and its errors went
  nowhere.** (`2da5507d`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/adapters/primary/transport/http/bridge.rs`) A
  client could `POST` faster than the upstream answered and the queue took
  all of it. It now holds 256 messages and answers `429` with `Retry-After`
  past that. A session whose loop ended in an error — an upstream that could
  not be reached, a client channel that failed — was dropped by `let _ =`;
  `with_session_report` hands it to the operator, and the `bridge` command
  prints it to stderr.

- **Eight rustdoc links named private or ambiguous items.** (`b7d73634`)
  `cargo doc` failed on the branch, and the lean `--no-default-features`
  build failed because the CLI read a library constant that only exists with
  `http`.

### Tests

- **Every definition of every revision round-trips.** (`fc097e9f`,
  `1828c10f`) The property suite covered 62 of 708 `(revision, definition)`
  pairs; `build.rs` now writes the table from the schemas themselves, so a
  revision that gains a definition gains a case. Field identifiers are
  pinned across all six revisions — no two members of an object collapse to
  one field, and every identifier is legal.

## Security model

The library is **default deny**:

- An `AuthContext` is a required parameter on every stateful
  port method. There is no path through the library that does
  not carry one.
- Authorization predicates are pure domain functions. The
  predicate that says "this user can see this resource" lives
  in `domain/`, not in an adapter; the adapter hands it the
  data and applies the answer.
- TLS verification is on by default. A `reqwest` client with
  certificate verification disabled is not constructed; the
  library has no path to do so.
- Path canonicalisation refuses a `..` traversal that escapes
  the allowed root with a typed error, not a panic.
- Tokens, Authorization headers, session ids in full, and
  elicitation responses are redacted at the tracing-layer
  boundary. The test that proves the redaction list is
  complete is `tests/secret_logging.rs`.

The full design, including what the library does *not* do
(token storage, rate limiting, CORS) and what the consumer is
responsible for, is in the
[Security model guide](https://greysquirr3l.github.io/protocol-droid/guides/security/)
on the docs site. The audit that backs the no-finding summary
in this policy is in
[`SECURITY-REVIEW.md`](https://github.com/greysquirr3l/protocol-droid/blob/main/SECURITY-REVIEW.md).

## Coordinated disclosure

A 90-day window is the default. A reporter who needs more time
(an embargoed CVE, a downstream rollout that takes longer than
the patch) names the date in the first message; the maintainer
confirms or counters. An embargo that runs past 180 days is
reviewed at 180 days; a longer embargo is honoured only if the
reporter and the maintainer agree in writing.

A patch lands **before** the advisory is public, and the
advisory text is shared with the reporter for review at least
48 hours before publication. The patch is credited in the
advisory, in the release notes, and in the git history; the
reporter's preferred attribution (name, handle, or anonymous)
is honoured.

### Changed

- **An HTTP server evicts a session that has been idle for 30 minutes.**
  (`2da5507d`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/adapters/primary/transport/http/serve/builder.rs`)
  A session used to live until the client sent `DELETE`. A client that opened
  sessions and left cost the server a map entry each time, and a bridge a
  task and an upstream connection each time, with no limit. `HttpBuilder`
  now sweeps by default; `with_idle_reaper` changes the window and
  `without_idle_reaper` restores the old behaviour. A client whose session
  was evicted gets `404` on its next request, which the specification tells
  it to answer by starting a new session — including one that held only a
  standing `GET` stream and sent nothing.

  `HttpBridge::with_idle_reaper` is opt-in, because the bridge is handed its
  store and cannot know what else shares it. It refuses a store built without
  `SessionStore::with_idle_reaper` rather than reaping nothing. The `bridge`
  command turns it on with a 30 minute default and `--idle-timeout 0` turns
  it off. `tokio/time` is now part of the `http` feature.

- **Every feature-matrix row cites the URL that documents it.** (`22cd58bf`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/domain/feature.rs`) 32 rows named a revision,
  12 an SEP number and one a URL, so a reader could follow almost none of
  them. Each row now carries a `citation`, and the same URL is in the doc
  comment on its `Feature` variant, with a test reading the file back to
  hold the two together.

### Changed

- **The cross-protocol bridge is two protocol adapters and one composition,
  not a hand-written translator for every pair of protocols.** (`2289b30c`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/protocol_adapter.rs`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/mcp_adapter.rs`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/a2a_adapter.rs`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/composed.rs`) The MCP ↔ A2A
  translation was a pair of functions that knew both vocabularies — one that
  turned `SendMessage` into `tools/call`, one that turned it back. A third
  protocol would have needed two more, and the pair nobody wrote about would
  have been the pair nobody tested.

  The translation now lives in per-protocol adapters behind a
  `ProtocolAdapter` seam, and `ComposedCodec` puts two of them together:
  lift on the way out, lower on the way back, with the IR in between. An
  adapter knows one protocol and does not mention the other, so a bridge
  between two protocols nobody wrote a translator for works the same way as
  the one that was.

  The IR gained the types the adapters meet at — `IrCall`, `IrMethod` and
  `IrOutcome` at `crates/protocol-droid/src/domain/ir/call.rs` — and a loss
  that has no counterpart on the other side is now recorded in the
  translation report rather than dropped in silence: an A2A part with no MCP
  counterpart, a task's artifacts, and structured content with no A2A
  counterpart are all reported.

  `CrossBridgePeer::new` lost its `downstream_side` parameter. The codec is
  built from a downstream adapter and an upstream adapter, so it knows which
  side it is; a caller that passed the side separately could disagree with
  the codec, and the disagreement would have shown up as a method the bridge

- **Token storage.** The `AuthorizationSecrets` port trait
